cases.case_name: In the Interest of Carlita B.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held the improvement periods and family case plans afforded the mother were more than adequate, and directed that abuse and neglect cases be given the highest priority with systems developed to monitor their progress and prevent delay.
cases.quote: Unjustified procedural delays wreak havoc on a child's development, stability and security.

relevance.INP-09: The Court ordered the Administrative Director to build systems monitoring the status and progress of abuse and neglect cases, the state-court analogue of systemic oversight triggers.
relevance.DEC-05: Once a petition opens a dependency case, Carlita B. makes prompt movement of that case a judicial obligation rather than an aspiration.
relevance.ACT-01: It measures the adequacy of services offered a family before compulsion, holding the services and plans here sufficient.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading WV authority on the adequacy of court-ordered improvement periods and the family case plans that implement them.
relevance.ACT-03: Delay in placement is treated as harm in itself, which frames how long a child may remain in foster care without resolution.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts are adequate when improvement periods and case plans give the parent a real, monitored opportunity to correct conditions.
relevance.PMC-01: Its directive to monitor case progress is the state-level counterpart to federal CFSR performance monitoring.
relevance.PMC-03: It supplies the WV courts' rationale for external monitoring of child-welfare case handling.
relevance.PMC-06: It supports analysis that keys system failure to measurable procedural delay.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of Tiffany Marie S.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming a finding of abuse and neglect, the Court held that a circuit court's findings of fact in an abuse and neglect case may be disturbed only if clearly erroneous, while its conclusions of law are reviewed de novo, and that the Department must prove the conditions existing when the petition was filed by clear and convincing proof.
cases.quote: absent a mistake of law, an appellate tribunal should disturb a circuit court's determination only if it is clearly erroneous

relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out or unfounded conclusion challenged on appeal is reviewed under this deferential standard for factual determinations.
relevance.DEC-03: It fixes the clear-and-convincing burden the Department carries to establish abuse or neglect as of the date of the petition.
relevance.OUT-05: Dismissal or non-substantiation rulings will stand unless the reviewing court is firmly convinced a mistake was made.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the standard-of-review framework governing every appellate reversal of a WV child-welfare determination.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: The Court held that DHHR kept its statutory responsibility for filing the case plan even after a private agency was made case manager, that foster parents may participate in abuse and neglect proceedings in a limited way, and that a child has a right to continued contact with those with whom he has formed a close bond when that serves his best interests.
cases.quote: we believe that DHHR nonetheless retained its statutory responsibility with regard to the filing of a case plan with the court under West Virginia Code § 49-6-5

relevance.DEC-06: Choosing a service route outside court compulsion does not shift the agency's statutory planning duties onto a contracted provider.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary or provider-delivered services do not discharge DHHR's own obligation to plan and document the family's case.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the WV authority that the statutory case-plan duty is the Department's and is non-delegable to a private case manager.
relevance.ACT-03: It also governs foster parents' limited right to participate and the placed child's interest in continued association with caregivers.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: The Court held that a child living in a home where another child was physically or sexually abused, and who is therefore at risk, is an 'abused child' under the statute, while declining to adopt any blanket rule that rights to all children in the home must be terminated.
cases.quote: there need not be a showing by the Department that each child in the home is directly abused, either sexually or physically, before termination of parental rights is sought

relevance.INP-10: Abuse of one child in the household is a lawful basis to escalate screening to investigation as to the other children.
relevance.DEC-03: It defines when a substantiated finding may extend to siblings who were not themselves directly harmed.
relevance.OUT-02: It allows termination as to at-risk siblings while forbidding an automatic, blanket termination for every child in the home.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reversing the return of an abused infant to his mother, the Court held that parental rights may be terminated where clear and convincing evidence shows extensive physical abuse in the parents' custody and the perpetrator remains unidentified, and it set out the duties of guardians ad litem.
cases.quote: There is no reasonable likelihood that the conditions of abuse can be substantially corrected because the perpetrator of Jeffrey R.L.'s physical abuse has not been identified

relevance.INP-07: Medical findings of extensive, unexplained injury to an infant are the evidentiary core of this kind of case.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification is not permissible where the abuser has never been identified and the parents will not identify him.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the leading WV case terminating rights on unexplained serious physical abuse of a child in parental custody.
relevance.OUT-06: It addresses the system's response when a child suffers serious injury and no perpetrator is identified.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming denial of post-adjudicatory and dispositional improvement periods and the termination of parental rights, the Court held that an improvement period is a carefully limited, discretionary opportunity that must be denied where granting it would jeopardize the child's best interests.
cases.quote: Where an improvement period would jeopardize the best interests of the child, for instance, an improvement period will not be granted

relevance.INP-05: A parent's own request for treatment-based services does not entitle her to the delay an improvement period would impose.
relevance.DEC-06: It marks the limits of the service-first path once the child's safety interest is engaged.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary participation in treatment does not compel the court to allow more time for services.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the WV standard governing whether court-ordered rehabilitative services (improvement periods) must be granted.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification services may be withheld where further delay for services would harm the child.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: The Court held that a parent who validly relinquished her parental rights lost her status as a 'parent' and therefore lacked standing to move under W. Va. Code § 49-6-6 for modification of the child's disposition, because a final termination order completely severs the parent-child relationship.
cases.quote: a final order terminating a person's parental rights, as the result of either an involuntary termination or a voluntary relinquishment of parental rights, completely severs the parent-child relationship

relevance.OUT-02: It fixes the legal consequence of termination, voluntary or involuntary, for any later attempt to undo it.
relevance.OUT-03: It explains why a terminated parent cannot later contest a guardianship or permanency disposition as a 'parent.'

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reversing the circuit court, the Court held that incarceration alone does not automatically terminate parental rights but the rights of an incarcerated parent may be terminated on a best-interests analysis, and that Rule 43's eighteen-month permanency deadline must be strictly followed.
cases.quote: Thus while the mere fact that someone is incarcerated will not result in automatic termination of parental rights, the parental rights of an incarcerated person may be terminated

relevance.OUT-01: An incarcerated parent's ability to correct conditions 'in the near future' is measured against the child's need for permanency, not the release date.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling WV authority on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming denial of a non-parent guardianship petition, the Court held that a court appointing a guardian under W. Va. Code § 44-10-3 must give priority to the child's mother or father, and that a family court presented with abuse and neglect allegations in a guardianship petition must refer the matter under Rule 48a(a).
cases.quote: In appointing a guardian, the court shall give priority to the minor's mother or father

relevance.INP-04: It is the WV rule requiring a family court that learns of abuse or neglect in a guardianship case to refer it into the child-protection track.
relevance.INP-05: A relative's guardianship petition is a common self-referral route into the system, and this case governs its handling.
relevance.ACT-04: Kinship guardianship cannot displace a fit parent's statutory priority.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the governing framework for guardianship as a permanency route in West Virginia.
relevance.OUT-04: Guardianship under Chapter 44 ends with minority, which frames what supports remain as a youth approaches majority.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: The Court held that a minor over fourteen who nominates a relative as guardian does not thereby permit a court to divest his fit, non-offending biological mother of custody, although the child may be entitled to visitation with the grandmother.
cases.quote: A court may not divest Gina H., Antonio's biological mother, of her custodial rights simply because Carol G. would be a "fit" guardian

relevance.INP-05: A child's or relative's own petition for guardianship cannot substitute for proof that the parent is unfit.
relevance.ACT-04: Kinship caregivers, even ones the child chooses, do not outrank a non-offending parent.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the leading WV case on contested guardianship as permanency against a biological parent.
relevance.OUT-04: It recognizes continued relationships with kin caregivers through visitation as the child approaches adulthood.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reversing a one-page order dismissing an abuse and neglect petition, the Court held that a circuit court that sees reasonable cause to believe additional abuse or neglect exists may compel DHHR to investigate and amend the petition, and must enter findings of fact and conclusions of law on the allegations.
cases.quote: the circuit court has the inherent authority to compel the Department to amend its petition to encompass the evidence or allegations

relevance.INP-01: The opinion sets out the reporting duties that attach when judicial officers have reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect.
relevance.INP-02: Repeated third-party referrals about a family are part of the record a court may require the agency to investigate.
relevance.INP-03: It describes the reporting and investigation loop among the courts, DHHR and the prosecutor.
relevance.INP-04: It is the WV authority for a judge ordering DHHR to investigate allegations the agency did not plead.
relevance.INP-06: Hotline referral history is relevant evidence the court may insist be developed.
relevance.INP-08: School and caregiver reports of risk fall within the allegations a court may require to be investigated.
relevance.INP-10: It compels escalation from an inadequate screening to a genuine investigation.
relevance.INP-12: The petition alleged imminent danger, and the Court required the danger allegations to be adjudicated rather than dropped.
relevance.DEC-01: A court may not let the agency screen out or abandon allegations without findings.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the principal WV check on an agency decision not to investigate further.
relevance.DEC-05: It defines the court's power over the content and scope of the agency's petition.
relevance.DEC-06: An agency preference for informal resolution cannot end a case without judicial findings.
relevance.ACT-05: It confirms the circuit court's inherent authority to order protective measures beyond what the agency requested.
relevance.OUT-05: It reverses a dismissal entered without evidentiary findings.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the model WV reversal of an agency-driven disposition for want of findings.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Diva P. v. Kaufman
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Denying the requested extraordinary relief, the Court held that the prosecuting attorney's statutory role in abuse and neglect matters is to cooperate with DHHR's civil action, and directed that the case plan prepared for the improvement period be submitted to the circuit court.
cases.quote: The legislature has specifically indicated through W.Va.Code § 49-6-10 that prosecutors must cooperate with DHHR's efforts to pursue civil abuse and neglect actions

relevance.INP-03: It defines how law enforcement and prosecutors interact with DHHR once maltreatment is suspected.
relevance.INP-04: It addresses who may invoke the court's authority in an abuse and neglect case and on what terms.
relevance.DEC-05: It governs the roles of prosecutor and Department in filing and maintaining the dependency petition, and requires the case plan to be filed with the court.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Answering a certified question from federal court, the Court held that West Virginia's mandatory child-abuse reporting statute, which carries criminal penalties, does not create an implied private civil cause of action against a mandated reporter who failed to report.
cases.quote: We conclude that relevant West Virginia law does not give rise to a private cause of action in this regard

relevance.INP-01: It is the controlling WV answer to what a failure by a mandated reporter does and does not give the child in civil court.
relevance.INP-02: It confines the reporting statute's enforcement to criminal penalties rather than private suit by any reporter or victim.
relevance.INP-06: It marks the legal consequence, or absence of one, when a report that should have been made to the hotline never was.
relevance.INP-07: Health-care and other mandated reporters face criminal, not implied civil, liability under the statute.
relevance.INP-08: The case arose from school employees who did not report suspected abuse of a student.
relevance.OUT-06: Where a child is seriously harmed after a missed report, this case limits the civil remedy available.
relevance.FAIL-04: It narrows the theories available against institutions after a maltreatment death or serious injury following non-reporting.
relevance.PMC-04: Accountability for non-reporting is legislative and criminal, which shapes what fatality review can actually change.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: The Court held that a public body answering a FOIA request must segregate or redact exempt material and disclose the rest, so the City had to produce redacted records even though the requester had not initially asked for redacted material, and it prescribed the Vaughn index and affidavit a body must supply when it withholds.
cases.quote: we conclude that the City was required to provide Mr. Farley this redacted material in response to his original FOIA request

relevance.INP-09: It is the practical tool by which oversight bodies and citizens force production of agency records.
relevance.FAIL-06: It defines what a public body must do, and prove, before withholding requested records.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review depends on the segregation-and-disclosure duty this case imposes.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the leading modern WV FOIA decision on redaction, the Vaughn index and de novo judicial review.
relevance.PMC-06: Systematic analysis of agency conduct rests on the records this decision makes obtainable.

cases.case_name: West Virginia Regional Jail & Correctional Facility Authority v. A.B.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: On rehearing the Court restated West Virginia's public-entity immunity framework and held the agency immune from vicarious liability for an employee's acts outside the scope of employment, and immune as to discretionary functions unless the plaintiff shows a violation of clearly established law or fraudulent, malicious or oppressive conduct.
cases.quote: we conclude that the WVRJCFA is entitled to immunity for respondent's claims based on vicarious liability for D. H.'s acts

relevance.OUT-06: It is the framework governing state-law damages claims against a state agency after a child in its care is harmed.
relevance.FAIL-04: It sets what a family must plead and prove to overcome DHHR immunity after a death or serious injury on the agency's watch.
relevance.FAIL-05: Claims of discriminatory or oppressive conduct by agency employees are tested against its clearly-established-law and malice standards.
relevance.PMC-02: It shapes the financial exposure, and therefore the accountability, of state child-welfare agencies.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review recommendations run up against the immunity doctrine this case consolidates.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reviewing challenges under the Indian Child Welfare Act to notice, active efforts, qualified expert testimony and placement, the Court found no ICWA violation and held the circuit court erred by declining to terminate, remanding for entry of an order terminating the parents' rights.
cases.quote: this Court finds no violation of the ICWA

relevance.INP-11: It is the leading published WV decision applying ICWA's notice, active-efforts, qualified-expert and placement requirements.
relevance.ACT-03: It reviews foster care placement of Indian children against 25 U.S.C. §§ 1912(e) and 1915(b).
relevance.FAIL-03: It shows how federal ICWA compliance is policed in WV courts and what a violation would have cost the case.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Delaware Tribe of Indians v. Nowicki-Eldridge
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Granting a writ of prohibition, the Court rejected the 'existing Indian family' exception, held ICWA governed the proceeding, found no good cause to deny transfer, and directed the circuit court to transfer jurisdiction to the Delaware Tribe's district court.
cases.quote: we find that the circuit court erred in denying the motion to transfer this action to the tribal court

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling WV authority on tribal jurisdiction and transfer under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(b).
relevance.ACT-04: Prospective kinship placements are subordinate to a properly invoked tribal transfer under ICWA.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to apply ICWA is treated as clear legal error correctable by extraordinary writ.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court noted that ICWA classifications rest on tribal political status, not impermissible racial discrimination.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Vacating and remanding, the Court held that a circuit court denying placement with a grandparent must enter detailed findings showing it considered the statutory grandparent preference and determined, on the whole record, that the preference was overcome by the child's best interests.
cases.quote: in denying grandparent placement the circuit court must make detailed findings of fact and conclusions of law demonstrating that it considered the grandparent preference

relevance.ACT-04: It is the current WV rule enforcing the grandparent placement preference in W. Va. Code § 49-4-114(a)(3).
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency through kinship cannot be rejected in a conclusory order.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a recent published reversal of a placement decision for inadequate findings.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reversing in part a permanency order, the Court held the circuit court lacked authority to order the Department of Human Services to pay the cost of transporting a child for post-permanency visitation with his psychological parents, and certainly not for years past his eighteenth birthday.
cases.quote: the circuit court had no authority to order the DHS to pay transportation costs for such visitation with psychological parents after permanency was achieved, let alone after A.E. turned eighteen

relevance.ACT-06: The case concerns a medically fragile child and marks the boundary of what care and support costs a court may impose on the agency.
relevance.OUT-04: It is the most recent WV authority on the limits of court-ordered agency obligations to a youth after permanency and past age eighteen.
relevance.PMC-02: It constrains judicially created spending obligations on the child-welfare agency, a point of intersection with audit and appropriations oversight.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Vacating the adjudicatory and dispositional orders, the Court held that a Rule 26(a) stipulated adjudication must contain agreed facts supporting court involvement and a statement of the respondent's problems, and that without a proper adjudication the circuit court had no jurisdiction to proceed to disposition.
cases.quote: Without properly made findings of abuse and/or neglect at adjudication, a case cannot proceed to disposition

relevance.DEC-01: An informal or undocumented resolution at the front of the case cannot substitute for adjudicatory findings.
relevance.DEC-03: A founded finding must be made on the record in the form the rules require, including for stipulations.
relevance.DEC-05: Opening the case is not enough; the adjudication stage must be completed correctly for the court to retain power.
relevance.OUT-05: Where adjudication was defective, the resulting orders are vacated and the case returns to the circuit court.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading recent WV vacatur for procedural failure in abuse and neglect proceedings.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of Lindsey C.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: The Court set aside an order terminating parental rights, holding that a guardian ad litem must be appointed for an adult respondent who is involuntarily hospitalized for mental illness, whether or not that respondent has been adjudicated incompetent.
cases.quote: in abuse and neglect proceedings the appointment of a guardian ad litem is required for adult respondents who are involuntarily hospitalized for mental illness

relevance.DEC-05: From the filing of the petition the court must ensure a hospitalized respondent is properly represented.
relevance.OUT-05: A termination entered without the required appointment cannot stand and the matter returns to the circuit court.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the WV case reversing a termination purely for a procedural-protection failure.

cases.case_name: Taylor v. West Virginia Department of Health & Human Resources
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment on the retaliatory discharge, Human Rights Act and false light claims of two discharged DHHR lawyers but reversing as to their Whistle-blower Law claims, the Court held that an employer's proffer of an arguably legitimate reason does not entitle it to summary judgment when the motive for the discharge is genuinely disputed.
cases.quote: There is little question that whether petitioners were discharged for retaliatory or discriminatory reasons is replete with disputed issues of material fact which must be resolved by the fact-finder

relevance.FAIL-05: It is the leading recent WV decision on retaliation and discrimination claims by employees of the child-welfare agency.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the WV whistle-blower framework protecting agency insiders who report wrongdoing about procurement and program conduct.
relevance.PMC-02: The underlying dispute concerned a DHHR contract award, the kind of transaction audits examine.
relevance.PMC-05: Protection for employees who disclose agency misconduct is a precondition of meaningful transparency.

cases.case_name: Jordan ex rel. Jordan v. Jackson
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The court upheld Virginia's emergency-removal statute facially and as applied, holding that a 65-hour weekend delay before judicial review of a child's emergency removal did not violate procedural due process, while allowing a separate municipal-liability claim to proceed under notice pleading.
cases.quote: it is well-settled that the requirements of process may be delayed where emergency action is necessary to avert imminent harm to a child

relevance.INP-03: The removal followed a report to the agency and a street encounter with the child, the paradigm referral-to-seizure sequence.
relevance.INP-12: It is the Fourth Circuit's controlling statement that protective custody may precede judicial review in a genuine emergency.
relevance.DEC-02: It describes the character of the inquiry a caseworker must make before acting on a report.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the governing circuit authority on how quickly an emergency removal must be reviewed by a court.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement following emergency removal is constitutional only within this framework of prompt judicial review.
relevance.ACT-05: Emergency protective action is permitted where needed to avert imminent harm, subject to prompt review.
relevance.ACT-06: Urgent protective intervention may precede process where delay would endanger the child.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal without emergency justification, or without prompt review, is where § 1983 liability begins in this circuit.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the county and its social workers, the court held that a social worker's investigative visit to a foster mother's home and the medical examinations of the children there did not violate the Fourth or Fourteenth Amendments, because such visits are judged by a balancing of the government's need against the intrusion.
cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

relevance.INP-07: It sustains medical examination of children suspected of being maltreated without criminal-law warrant standards.
relevance.INP-10: It defines the constitutional room a worker has when escalating from report to in-home assessment.
relevance.INP-12: It is the Fourth Circuit's baseline on caseworker entry and observation preceding protective action.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the controlling circuit authority on the reasonableness of CPS home visits during an investigation.
relevance.DEC-04: Observations lawfully made on such a visit are the evidentiary basis for an emergency removal decision.
relevance.ACT-06: It addresses the constitutionality of examining children medically during a child-protection investigation.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the line between a lawful investigative entry and an unreasonable search supporting a § 1983 claim.

cases.case_name: Weller v. Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming dismissal as to the agency but reversing as to individual caseworkers, the court held a parent is entitled to a hearing before being deprived of custody and that, where emergency action is taken first, the State must promptly initiate judicial proceedings to ratify it.
cases.quote: the state has the burden to initiate prompt judicial proceedings to ratify its emergency action

relevance.INP-12: It places the burden on the State, not the parent, to get an emergency custody decision before a judge.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Fourth Circuit rule that an emergency removal must be promptly ratified by a court.
relevance.ACT-05: Emergency protective measures survive only if the State moves quickly for judicial ratification.
relevance.FAIL-02: Months of custody without a ratifying hearing states a due process claim against the individual workers.

cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the social workers, the court held that conduct that was at most negligent in bringing about the children's removal cannot support a § 1983 claim, so the defendants were entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: Because a § 1983 claim cannot be sustained, it follows that the defendants are entitled to qualified immunity

relevance.INP-03: The case began with a school-based referral to child protective services, illustrating the referral pathway.
relevance.INP-08: The investigation was triggered by the child's school attendance and the school's report.
relevance.INP-10: It follows a report through screening into a CINA petition and shelter care.
relevance.INP-12: It illustrates how protective custody obtained through the court is reviewed after the fact.
relevance.DEC-01: Errors and miscommunications in agency handling are judged by more than negligence before liability attaches.
relevance.DEC-02: The workers' investigation and petition were held not to violate constitutional rights.
relevance.DEC-04: It addresses the consequences when children are removed on inaccurate information.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the Fourth Circuit's limit on § 1983 wrongful-removal claims: negligence is not enough.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may irrevocably sever the rights of parents in their natural child, the Due Process Clause requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: It is the federal constitutional floor for the proof that must ultimately support a maltreatment finding used to sever parental rights.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling federal standard of proof for termination of parental rights, mirrored in W. Va. Code § 49-4-604.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the Constitution does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every termination proceeding, leaving that decision to the trial court in the first instance subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

relevance.OUT-02: It sets the federal constitutional floor for counsel at termination, above which West Virginia's statutory right to appointed counsel operates.
relevance.FAIL-01: Claims that a parent was unrepresented or poorly represented on appeal are measured against this federal baseline plus WV's broader statutory right.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that States make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and reunify families does not create a right enforceable by beneficiaries through § 1983 or an implied right of action.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

relevance.INP-09: Enforcement of federal child-welfare standards runs through federal administrative oversight, not private suits.
relevance.INP-11: It illustrates that federal funding conditions differ from statutes like ICWA that create expressly enforceable rights.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the controlling authority that Title IV-E compliance failures are remedied federally, not by private damages actions.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR and federal fiscal review are the practical remedies for state non-performance under this decision.
relevance.PMC-06: Analysis of non-compliance must target federal monitoring and funding levers rather than litigation by families.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, so the agency's failure to remove Joshua from his abusive father was not a constitutional violation.
cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.INP-01: Reports received and not acted on do not, without more, create federal constitutional liability for the agency.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the controlling authority when a child dies or is gravely injured after the agency knew of the danger but left the child at home.
relevance.FAIL-02: It frames the asymmetry: removal is state action subject to the Constitution, while failure to remove generally is not.
relevance.FAIL-03: Federal remedies for agency inaction lie in statutory and administrative oversight, not the Due Process Clause.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the first hurdle in any federal claim arising from a child's death under agency supervision, subject to the special-relationship and state-created-danger exceptions the Court left open.
relevance.PMC-01: Because constitutional damages are largely foreclosed, federal performance review carries the accountability burden.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights where an infant was allowed to reach near-starvation, the Court held that compelling circumstances justified denying an improvement period and that immediate termination, without first employing a less drastic intervening alternative, is more reasonable where the child is under the age of three.
cases.quote: where a child is under the age of three immediate termination without an intervening period employing a less drastic alternative is more reasonable than in other cases

relevance.OUT-01: It fixes the point at which continued effort toward reunification becomes futile, holding that insisting on an improvement period here would have been a vain act because return of the child might have threatened her life.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the foundational West Virginia termination standard, quoted as controlling in both Jeffrey R.L. and Charity H., permitting termination without intervening less restrictive alternatives and tying the permissible wait to the child's age and vulnerability.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Holding that the lower tribunals abused their discretion by failing to apply the statutory grandparent preference, the Court remanded with directions that the child be placed with his paternal grandparents for adoption following a gradual transition of custody.
cases.quote: the preference for grandparent placement may be overcome only where the record reviewed in its entirety establishes that such placement is not in the best interests of the child

relevance.ACT-04: It is the rule In re A.F. applies: the statutory grandparent preference is presumptively in the child's best interests and can be defeated only on the record as a whole, not on an adoption committee's unexplored misgivings.
relevance.OUT-03: It governs when kinship placement must be chosen over a non-relative foster home as the child's permanent home, and requires the agency to actually assist relatives in developing a permanency plan.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Remanding for a proper adjudicatory hearing, the Court held that a circuit court may not reach any dispositional alternative until it has held a hearing and determined whether the child is abused or neglected, and that a voluntary arrangement among the parties cannot bypass that threshold question.
cases.quote: have determined "whether such child is abused or neglected." Such a finding is the prerequisite to any further proceedings in the case.

relevance.DEC-03: It is the origin of the rule In re Z.S. enforces: the adjudicatory finding of abuse or neglect is the gateway every founded determination must pass through before the court may act.
relevance.DEC-05: The statutory structure requires a completed adjudicatory hearing under the abuse-and-neglect article before the case that the petition opened can move to any disposition.
relevance.DEC-06: A voluntary dispositional plan is permitted only with court approval and cannot be used by the parties or the agency to circumvent the threshold abuse-or-neglect question.
relevance.ACT-05: The opinion restates the statutory predicates for any emergency taking short of adjudication — imminent danger to the child's physical well-being and no reasonably available alternative to removal.
relevance.OUT-05: If the evidence is insufficient to warrant a finding of abuse or neglect, the statute directs the court to dismiss the petition.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights but reversing the summary denial of post-termination visitation, the Court held that the circuit court did not err in refusing to extend the improvement period or order long-term foster care where no evidence showed a reasonable likelihood of improvement.
cases.quote: Given the lack of any evidence showing a reasonable likelihood of improvement, we find no error in the circuit court's refusal to extend the respondent's improvement period

relevance.ACT-02: It is the controlling WV decision on court-ordered rehabilitative services — the family case plan that implements an improvement period, the permissible length of that period, and the parent's own statutory responsibility for initiating and completing its terms.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. West Virginia Department of Human Services v. Cheryl M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reversing termination of parental rights, the Court held that the mother was entitled to a meaningful improvement period absent compelling circumstances and that DHS failed to comply with W. Va. Code § 49-6D-3 by never preparing a court-approved family case plan or rendering good-faith assistance under it.
cases.quote: when an improvement period is authorized, then the court by order shall require the DHS to prepare a family case plan pursuant to W.Va.Code, 49-6D-3 (1984)

relevance.ACT-01: It holds the agency to actually delivering good-faith assistance and counseling, faulting DHS for moving for total severance before any parenting help had been extended to the mother.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the WV authority, relied on in Diva P. and discussed in Charity H., that a court-ordered improvement period must be accompanied by a court-approved family case plan supplying detailed, measurable standards against which improvement can be judged.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Denying the requested writ with directions, the Court held that custody was properly restored to the fit natural father over the stepfather who had been caring for the child, and directed the circuit court to confer visitation on the stepfather and half-brother with whom the child had formed close bonds.
cases.quote: There being no showing of unfitness or abandonment before us, we find that the circuit court did not err in restoring the custody of Elizabeth to her natural father

relevance.ACT-04: It is the rule underlying both In re Jonathan G. and In re Antonio R.A.: a kin or de facto caregiver's attachment to the child cannot displace a parent who has not been shown unfit, abandoning, immoral or otherwise derelict.
relevance.OUT-04: It recognizes the child's own right to continued contact with the caregivers she considers family as custody shifts, the interest that supports maintaining those relationships as a youth grows toward independence.

cases.case_name: Elmer Jimmy S. v. Kenneth B.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming denial of the paternal grandparents' visitation petition, the Court held that although circuit courts have jurisdiction to consider grandparent visitation even after the related parent's rights are terminated, the terminated parent cannot satisfy the statute's 'noncustodial parent' requirement because the law no longer recognizes him as a parent.
cases.quote: Thus, the non-parent whose parental rights have been terminated could not then be deemed a "noncustodial parent."

relevance.OUT-03: It is the authority on which In re Cesar L. expressly builds its syllabus point: once rights are terminated the law no longer recognizes that individual as a 'parent,' which controls who may claim parental status in a later guardianship, visitation or permanency dispute.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held that the Department bears a burden that never shifts to the parent — to prove by clear and convincing evidence the conditions of neglect existing when the petition was filed — and that a bare recital of statutory language does not satisfy the findings requirement, although that error was waived here.
cases.quote: The proper question is whether the evidence which the State Department of Welfare did present was clear and convincing proof of neglect existing at the time the petition was filed.

relevance.DEC-03: It is the origin of the burden the brief otherwise attributes to Tiffany Marie S.: a founded finding must rest on clear and convincing proof of conditions existing at the time of the petition, and the burden remains on the Department throughout, even during an improvement period.
relevance.DEC-05: It holds that the court deciding the case must enter real findings of fact and conclusions of law rather than reciting the statutory disposition language, though an unpreserved objection to that failure is waived.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Vacating the termination order and remanding, the Court held that a circuit court may not terminate parental rights without first adjudicating the parent as having abused or neglected the child, where the same court had expressly concluded three months earlier that the father had not abused or neglected them.
cases.quote: a circuit court may not terminate a parent's rights to his child without first finding that the parent abused or neglected his child

relevance.DEC-01: An allegation the court has rejected cannot be carried forward into disposition; where the agency's theory of abuse or neglect fails, the case must end at adjudication rather than proceed on the agency's preference.
relevance.DEC-05: Filing and litigating a petition does not by itself empower the court to act on the child's placement; it is the adjudicatory finding, not the petition, that supplies the authority to dispose of the case.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Vacating both dispositional orders, the Court held that the fifteen-of-twenty-two-months filing trigger does not relieve the Department of presenting, or the circuit court of finding, affirmative evidence supporting termination, and that the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a child who did not meet the statutory definition of an abused or neglected child.
cases.quote: Because B.S. was not an abused or neglected child, the circuit court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to address, and ultimately terminate, the petitioner's parental rights to this child

relevance.DEC-01: It is the recent WV authority, relied on in In re Z.S., on what an adjudication must actually establish: a child safely placed with non-abusing legal guardians before the petition does not meet the statutory definition, and the case as to that child should never have gone forward.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the statutory definition of an abused or neglected child is not met, the orders as to that child are vacated for want of jurisdiction and the matter returns to the circuit court.

cases.case_name: In re E.H., J.S., E.K., and C.K.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Vacating the dispositional order and remanding, the Court held that an order terminating parental rights that lacks the findings of fact and conclusions of law required by Rule 36(a) and W. Va. Code § 49-4-604 cannot support termination and must be vacated.
cases.quote: we agree with Petitioner that the December 27, 2021 dispositional order does not contain the requisite findings of fact or conclusions of law to support termination of his parental rights

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the recent published WV reversal cited in In re A.F. for a dispositional order too vague to permit meaningful appellate review — a bare invocation of 'aggravated circumstances' with no supporting findings.
relevance.OUT-05: A disposition entered without the findings the rules require is set aside in its entirety and the case returned to the circuit court for a proper order.

cases.case_name: Daily Gazette Co. v. West Virginia Development Office
cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Remanding with directions, the Court held that a public body withholding records under the internal-memoranda exemption must produce a Vaughn index justifying each document and a supporting affidavit, and that the exemption covers only deliberative advice, opinions and recommendations, not ordinary communications with private parties.
cases.quote: The Vaughn index must provide a relatively detailed justification as to why each document is exempt, specifically identifying the reasons why W. Va.Code, 29B-1-4(8) [1977] is relevant

relevance.INP-09: Oversight of an agency begins with its records, and this decision sets out precisely what the agency must establish, document by document, before it may withhold them.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the foundational WV FOIA rule — that the withholding body bears the burden and may not rely on conclusory or general assertions — which Farley v. Worley later extends to segregation and redaction.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review of child-welfare policy depends on the itemized, document-by-document justification this case requires of any public body claiming an exemption.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the West Virginia decision establishing the Vaughn index requirement that sits at the centre of state transparency practice.
relevance.PMC-06: Systematic analysis of agency conduct depends on records that cannot be withheld on unexplained assertions of deliberative privilege.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Reversing a jury verdict and ordering the action dismissed, the Court held that qualified or statutory immunity turns on whether the conduct violated a constitutional or statutory right that was clearly established at the time, and that the plaintiff produced no affirmative evidence of improper motive or intent to harm sufficient to reach a fact-finder.
cases.quote: we follow a two-part test: (1) does the alleged conduct set out a constitutional or statutory violation, and (2) were the constitutional standards clearly established at the time in question?

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the WV qualified-immunity framework a caseworker invokes against a state-court damages claim for an unlawful removal, and it makes the 'clearly established' question one of law for the court.
relevance.FAIL-04: It, rather than the jail case, is the primary WV immunity authority expressly incorporated into WVRJCFA v. A.B.'s syllabus, and so states what a family must overcome after a child dies or is seriously injured under agency supervision.
relevance.FAIL-05: Allegations of discriminatory or retaliatory motive by agency officials must be supported by affirmative evidence of improper motive and intent to harm, not conclusory pleading.
relevance.OUT-06: It fixes what a plaintiff must plead and prove before a public body or its officials answer in damages for harm to a child.
relevance.PMC-02: Immunity doctrine sets the financial exposure that audit and oversight findings can actually be converted into, and this case consolidates that doctrine for West Virginia.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held that the trial court did not err in refusing an improvement period the mother first requested after the final hearing, and that sufficient evidence supported the finding of no reasonable likelihood that the conditions of neglect could be substantially corrected.
cases.quote: In view of this delay and of the failure to make a timely request, we find that the trial court did not err in refusing an improvement period.

relevance.ACT-02: It is the WV authority that the statutory entitlement to court-ordered rehabilitative services is forfeited unless the parent moves for an improvement period before the final hearing, and it applies the R.J.M. least-restrictive-alternative standard in affirming termination.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights and the denial of post-termination visitation, the Court held that parents who made no serious effort during a granted improvement period and refused to cooperate with the Department's repeated attempts to help could not show a reasonable likelihood that the conditions of abuse and neglect would be corrected.
cases.quote: Although they were granted an improvement period, the appellants made no serious effort to change their behavior or provide a stable home for their children.

relevance.OUT-01: Cited alongside R.J.M. in Charity H., it measures reunification by what the parents actually did with the improvement period they were given, against the Department's repeated attempts to help them regain custody.

notes: Method: every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session (search + /opinions/<id>/ full text) and its text read. Every quote was verified programmatically as an exact whitespace/quote-normalized substring of the retrieved opinion text, taken from the majority or lead opinion body (never a syllabus point, headnote, dissent or concurrence).

IMPORTANT WEST VIRGINIA CAVEAT FOR LAWYERS: in West Virginia the 'Syllabus by the Court' points, not the body text, are the Court's authoritative statements of law (W. Va. Const. art. VIII, § 4). Because the task forbids quoting syllabi, the quotes here come from the opinions' analysis. When citing these cases in a brief, pull the corresponding syllabus points (e.g., Syl. Pt. 1, Tiffany Marie S.; Syl. Pts. 2 & 7, Carlita B.; Syl. Pt. 2, R.J.M.; Syl. Pt. 3, Katie S.; Syl. Pt. 3, Cecil T.).

No published WV authority was located, despite targeted searches, on: administrative due process for a substantiated finding or placement on a central child-abuse registry; differential/alternative response; CPS-specific protective orders; authorization of emergency medical or psychological treatment over parental objection; extended foster care/Chafee services to age 21; and missing or absent children from foster care. Those nodes are populated with the nearest on-point authority (constitutional removal/emergency cases, In re A.E. for post-18 agency obligations) and the federal standard; treat them as gaps, not as settled WV law.

In re Katie S., 198 W. Va. 79, 479 S.E.2d 589 (1996) and In re Christina W., 219 W. Va. 678, 639 S.E.2d 770 (2006) were retrieved and read but omitted: their operative rules (family case plan requirements; a guardian ad litem's qualified duty of confidentiality) appear only in syllabus points, and the CourtListener body text of both is OCR-corrupted at the relevant sentences. Both remain good law and are worth citing for ACT-02 (case plans) and records/confidentiality questions respectively.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the WV node files are almost entirely recent memorandum decisions with synthetic citations; all were discarded except that the ICWA entry pointed to the published Delaware Tribe writ opinion, which was retrieved and retained.

West Virginia's Intermediate Court of Appeals (court_id wvactapp, created 2022) does not hear child abuse and neglect appeals — they go directly to the Supreme Court of Appeals — and searches of wvactapp produced no published decision on any of these doctrines. Hence no intermediate appellate authority is cited.

Citations: CourtListener clusters for the 2019-2026 WV opinions (In re N.R., Delaware Tribe, In re Z.S.-1, In re A.F., In re A.E.) carry no reporter citation, so slip form is used. In re N.R. is reported at 242 W. Va. 581, 836 S.E.2d 799 (that parallel citation appears in the text of the Delaware Tribe opinion retrieved here). In re Z.S.-1 is a consolidated appeal, Nos. 22-602 and 22-0478.

Dates: date_decided follows the decision date stated in the opinion where CourtListener's cluster date_filed reflects a submission, dissent-filing or import date (In re Lindsey C., decided Dec. 14, 1995, is dated 1996-07-19 in the cluster; Santosky's cluster date is 1982-02-22 though the opinion was decided Mar. 24, 1982). Wildauer and Weller each exist in duplicate CourtListener clusters (606677 and 540031 carry the F.2d decision dates used here, 1993-05-05 and 1990-04-24); the cluster_ids given are the Harvard-text clusters whose opinions were actually read.

§ 1983 / wrongful removal: West Virginia sits in the Fourth Circuit, so Jordan, Weller, Wildauer and Martin are the controlling federal authorities for FAIL-02, INP-12 and DEC-04. Parallel state-law damages claims against DHHR/DoHS are governed by the immunity framework of W. Va. Reg'l Jail & Corr. Facility Auth. v. A.B. (a jail case, but the Court's consolidated statement of public-entity immunity, applied to all state agencies).

Additional holdings worth knowing but not quoted: In re Cecil T. also holds that Rule 43's eighteen-month permanency deadline must be strictly followed absent extraordinary, record-substantiated circumstances (relevant to ACT-03, OUT-01, OUT-03); In re Jeffrey R.L. also sets guardian ad litem duties including the duty to exercise the children's appellate rights (relevant to FAIL-01); In re Randy H. also describes Rule 48 of the Family Court Rules, which obliges a family court judge with reasonable cause to suspect abuse to report to DHHR and the circuit court (relevant to INP-04).

Statutory renumbering: opinions before 2015 cite the former W. Va. Code §§ 49-6-1 et seq.; those provisions are now §§ 49-4-601 et seq. (e.g., former § 49-6-5 dispositions = current § 49-4-604; former § 49-6A-2 mandatory reporting = current § 49-2-803). The node files cite the current numbering.

Missing (for a later pass): In re R.J.M., 164 W. Va. 496, 266 S.E.2d 114 (1980) — the foundational WV termination standard (termination without less-restrictive alternatives where there is no reasonable likelihood conditions of abuse or neglect can be substantially corrected; courts need not exhaust every speculative possibility of parental improvement). It is quoted as controlling in two cases the brief does include (Jeffrey R.L. and Charity H.) yet is itself absent from OUT-01, OUT-02 and ACT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): Napoleon S. v. Walker, 217 W. Va. 254, 617 S.E.2d 801 (2005) — the grandparent-placement preference is presumptively in the child's best interests and may be overcome only on the record as a whole. In re A.F. is built directly on its Syllabus Point 4; ACT-04 and OUT-03 cite the 2025 application without the rule it applies.

Missing (for a later pass): State v. T.C., 172 W. Va. 47, 303 S.E.2d 685 (1983) — a determination that the child is abused or neglected is a prerequisite to any dispositional alternative. This is the rule In re Z.S. enforces; DEC-03 and DEC-05 should cite it directly.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Katie S., 198 W. Va. 79, 479 S.E.2d 589 (1996) — the controlling WV requirements for the DHHR family case plan. The brief's own notes concede it was read and omitted because its rule lives in the syllabus; ACT-02 is incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel. W. Va. Dep't of Human Servs. v. Cheryl M., 177 W. Va. 688, 356 S.E.2d 181 (1987) — improvement periods and the Department's duty to prepare a family case plan under W. Va. Code 49-6D-3. Relied on in Diva P. (Syl. Pt. 3) and in Charity H.'s discussion of the pre-1996 presumption; absent from ACT-01 and ACT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): Honaker v. Burnside, 182 W. Va. 448, 388 S.E.2d 322 (1989) — although custody belongs with the natural parent absent abandonment, misconduct or neglect, the child may have a right to continued visitation with a third party with whom a close bond has formed. It is the rule underlying both In re Jonathan G. and In re Antonio R.A.; absent from ACT-04, OUT-03 and OUT-04.

Missing (for a later pass): Elmer Jimmy S. v. Kenneth B., 199 W. Va. 263, 483 S.E.2d 846 (1997) — once parental rights are terminated the law no longer recognizes the individual as a 'parent.' Cesar L. expressly builds its new syllabus point on this case; OUT-02 and OUT-03 should carry it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Interest of S.C., 168 W. Va. 366, 284 S.E.2d 867 (1981) — the Department must prove conditions existing at the time of filing by clear and convincing evidence. It is the origin of the burden the brief attributes to Tiffany Marie S.; belongs at DEC-03.

Missing (for a later pass): In re A.P.-1, 241 W. Va. 688, 827 S.E.2d 830 (2019) — adjudicatory findings of abuse and neglect and their required form; cited as controlling in In re Z.S. and directly relevant to DEC-03 and FAIL-01.

Missing (for a later pass): In re C.S., 247 W. Va. 212, 875 S.E.2d 350 (2022) — recent WV authority on what an adjudication must establish, relied on in In re Z.S.; DEC-01 and DEC-03 are thin without it.

Missing (for a later pass): In re E.H., 247 W. Va. 456, 880 S.E.2d 922 (2022) — reversal of a dispositional order that was 'simply too vague' to permit meaningful appellate review; cited in In re A.F. and directly on point for FAIL-01.

Missing (for a later pass): Daily Gazette Co. v. W. Va. Development Office, 198 W. Va. 563, 482 S.E.2d 180 (1996) — the WV FOIA decision establishing the Vaughn index requirement that Farley v. Worley extends. PMC-05 and FAIL-06 cite the extension without the foundation.

Missing (for a later pass): Hutchison v. City of Huntington, 198 W. Va. 139, 479 S.E.2d 649 (1996) — the WV qualified/statutory immunity framework for public officials and political subdivisions, expressly incorporated into WVRJCFA v. A.B.'s syllabus. It, not the jail case, is the primary authority for FAIL-04 and OUT-06 immunity analysis.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Jonathan P., 182 W. Va. 302, 387 S.E.2d 537 (1989) — least-restrictive-alternative analysis in termination, quoted through Jeffrey R.L.'s Syllabus Point 1; relevant to OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Erica C., 214 W. Va. 375, 589 S.E.2d 517 (2003) — improvement periods and a parent's inability to demonstrate correction of underlying conditions, cited alongside R.J.M. in Charity H.; relevant to ACT-02 and OUT-01.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-21): all fifteen authorities the verifier named as missing were searched for on CourtListener, retrieved as full opinion text and read in this session. All fifteen are real, published and on point; all fifteen are now added. The 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes immediately above are retained verbatim as the prior state of the brief but are now SUPERSEDED by the additions recorded below.

Added In re R.J.M., 164 W. Va. 496, 266 S.E.2d 114 (1980) (cluster 8217537) for OUT-01 and OUT-02: it is the foundational WV termination standard that Jeffrey R.L. and Charity H. quote as controlling, permitting termination without an intervening less drastic alternative and tying the permissible wait to a child under three.

Added Napoleon S. v. Walker, 217 W. Va. 254, 617 S.E.2d 801 (2005) (cluster 1366628) for ACT-04 and OUT-03: it supplies the presumptive grandparent-placement preference — overcome only on the record reviewed in its entirety — that In re A.F. (2025) merely applies.

Added State v. T.C., 172 W. Va. 47, 303 S.E.2d 685 (1983) (cluster 8217726) for DEC-03, DEC-05, DEC-06, ACT-05 and OUT-05: it is the source of the rule In re Z.S. enforces, that an adjudicatory finding of abuse or neglect is the prerequisite to any disposition, and it holds that a voluntary arrangement among the parties cannot circumvent that threshold — the closest published WV authority to a differential/alternative-response limit.

Added In re Katie S., 198 W. Va. 79, 479 S.E.2d 589 (1996) (cluster 1374294) for ACT-02: the previously omitted case-plan/improvement-period authority. Its family case plan rule does live in the syllabus (Syl. Pts. 3 and 4), so the quote used here is the Court's own body-text holding that an improvement period need not be extended absent evidence of a reasonable likelihood of improvement; cite the syllabus points for the case-plan requirements themselves.

Added State ex rel. W. Va. Dep't of Human Servs. v. Cheryl M., 177 W. Va. 688, 356 S.E.2d 181 (1987) (cluster 1325257) for ACT-01 and ACT-02: it holds that a court-ordered improvement period triggers a mandatory, court-approved family case plan under W. Va. Code § 49-6D-3 and reverses a termination where DHS instead pressed for severance before offering meaningful assistance.

Added Honaker v. Burnside, 182 W. Va. 448, 388 S.E.2d 322 (1989) (cluster 1390972) for ACT-04 and OUT-04: it is the rule underlying both In re Jonathan G. and In re Antonio R.A. — custody belongs with the fit natural parent, but the child retains an interest in continued contact with the caregivers with whom she has bonded.

Added Elmer Jimmy S. v. Kenneth B., 199 W. Va. 263, 483 S.E.2d 846 (1997) (cluster 1364518) for OUT-03: it is the authority on which In re Cesar L. builds, holding that a person whose parental rights have been terminated can no longer be treated as a 'parent' for statutory purposes.

Added In the Interest of S.C., 168 W. Va. 366, 284 S.E.2d 867 (1981) (cluster 1302179) for DEC-03 and DEC-05: it is the origin of the clear-and-convincing, conditions-at-the-time-of-filing burden the brief previously attributed to Tiffany Marie S., and it holds that the burden never shifts to the parent, even during an improvement period.

Added In re A.P.-1, A.P.-2, A.P.-3, 825 S.E.2d 324 (W. Va. 2019) (cluster 4599903) for DEC-01 and DEC-05: it vacates a termination entered after the same circuit court had found no abuse or neglect, holding that adjudication is an absolute precondition to termination.

Added In re C.S. and B.S., No. 21-0694 (W. Va. June 15, 2022) (cluster 6478070) for DEC-01 and OUT-05: it is the recent WV authority on what an adjudication must establish, holding the circuit court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a child who did not meet the statutory definition and that the fifteen-of-twenty-two-months filing trigger does not excuse affirmative proof.

Added In re E.H., J.S., E.K., and C.K., No. 22-0067 (W. Va. Nov. 17, 2022) (cluster 8512342) for FAIL-01 and OUT-05: it is the vacatur, cited in In re A.F., of a dispositional order too vague to permit meaningful appellate review.

Va. 139, 479 S.E.2d 649 (1996) (cluster 1374249) for FAIL-02, FAIL-04, FAIL-05, OUT-06 and PMC-02: it is the WV qualified/statutory immunity framework expressly incorporated into WVRJCFA v. Va. 302, 387 S.E.2d 537 (1989) (cluster 1261163) for ACT-02: it applies the R.J.M. least-restrictive-alternative standard and holds that the statutory entitlement to an improvement period is forfeited if not requested before the final hearing. Note for lawyers: the R.J.M. least-restrictive-alternative rule appears in Jonathan P. only as a quotation of R.J.M.'s syllabus point, so the quote used here is the Court's own improvement-period holding; cite R.J.M. node_map is capped at six authorities per node, ranked leading-authority-first, as required. Where a case's relevance object names a node whose index is already full, the case entry still records that relevance (it is real) but the index lists only the six strongest authorities. This affects a small number of pairings, chiefly on DEC-05 (In re Lindsey C.), OUT-05 (In re Lindsey C.) and FAIL-01 (Lassiter).

node_map has also been reconciled against the case entries' relevance objects, which previously diverged: DEC-06, ACT-01, ACT-05, ACT-06, INP-01, INP-03, INP-05, INP-11, INP-12, ACT-03, DEC-04, FAIL-03 and OUT-04 each gained entries for cases whose relevance already named those nodes but which the index omitted.

One deliberate substitution in node_map: In re Christina L. (1342969) was removed from OUT-02 to make room for In re R.J.M. within the six-case cap. Christina L. remains in the brief and is indexed at INP-10 and DEC-03, which are its stronger nodes; its OUT-02 relevance sentence is retained in its case entry.

After this pass all 42 nodes carry between 2 and 6 cases and the brief contains 45 distinct cases. DEC-06 (differential/alternative response) is still the weakest node: State v. T.C. is the closest published WV authority, and it addresses voluntary dispositional arrangements inside a filed case rather than a formal differential-response track. West Virginia has no published appellate decision construing a differential-response programme; treat that as a genuine gap.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel. Miller v. Locke, 162 W. Va. 946, 253 S.E.2d 540 (1979) — the WV standard for an emergency taking (imminent danger to the child's physical well-being AND no reasonably available alternative to removal), quoted as controlling in State v. T.C. at the very passage the brief relies on. This is the most serious remaining gap: ACT-05, DEC-04 and INP-12 are populated almost entirely with Fourth Circuit authority and carry no WV emergency-custody rule at all.

Missing (for a later pass): W. Va. Dep't of Health & Human Res. ex rel. Wright v. Doris S., 197 W. Va. 489, 475 S.E.2d 865 (1996) — the leading WV authority that a parent's failure to acknowledge the existence of the problem renders it untreatable and forecloses any reasonable likelihood of correction. It is among the most-cited WV abuse-and-neglect decisions and is absent from ACT-02, OUT-01 and OUT-02, which currently reach that question only obliquely through Erica C. and Katie S.

Missing (for a later pass): In re K.L., 233 W. Va. 547, 759 S.E.2d 778 (2014) — the modern restatement (Syl. Pt. 4) of the rule that the burden of proof in an abuse and neglect case never shifts from the Department and remains on it throughout. In re C.S. quotes it as controlling for exactly the proposition DEC-03 currently sources only to the 1981 S.C. decision.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Christina W., 219 W. Va. 678, 639 S.E.2d 770 (2006) — the guardian ad litem's qualified duty of confidentiality and the handling of abuse-and-neglect records. The brief's own notes concede it was retrieved and read but omitted because its rule lives in the syllabus; that is not a reason to leave FAIL-06 and PMC-05 without the one WV decision that addresses child-welfare record confidentiality as opposed to general FOIA.

Missing (for a later pass): Associated Press v. Canterbury, 224 W. Va. 708, 688 S.E.2d 317 (2009) — the leading modern WV FOIA decision on when records in a public official's possession relate to the conduct of the public's business and on the personal-privacy exemption analysis. PMC-05 and FAIL-06 currently stop at 1996 and 2004; Canterbury is what a practitioner would be asked about first.

Missing (for a later pass): James M. v. Maynard, 185 W. Va. 648, 408 S.E.2d 400 (1991) — gradual transition of permanent custody (Syl. Pt. 3) and the guardian ad litem's duties continuing until permanent placement. It is quoted as controlling in Napoleon S., which the brief now includes, and is directly relevant to ACT-04, OUT-03 and FAIL-01.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Lacey P., 189 W. Va. 580, 433 S.E.2d 518 (1993) — courts are not required to exhaust every speculative possibility of parental improvement where the child's welfare is seriously threatened. Quoted in Katie S. at the passage the brief uses; belongs at OUT-01 and OUT-02 alongside R.J.M.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Carol B., 209 W. Va. 658, 550 S.E.2d 636 (2001) — the guardian ad litem's duty of full and independent investigation, including interviewing all prospective placements when placement is at issue. Cited in Napoleon S.; relevant to ACT-04 and FAIL-01, where GAL failure is a recurring reversal ground the brief reaches only through Jeffrey R.L.

Missing (for a later pass): In re K.S., 246 W. Va. 517, 874 S.E.2d 319 (2022) — recent syllabus authority on the findings a dispositional order must contain; cited as controlling in In re E.H., which the brief now includes. FAIL-01 and OUT-05 would be stronger with the source rule as well as its application.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Timber M., 231 W. Va. 44, 743 S.E.2d 352 (2013) — modern restatement of both the grandparent-placement preference and the failure-to-acknowledge rule; frequently the first case cited in current WV briefing on ACT-04 and OUT-01, and absent here.
